query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A post‐casting aging treatment designed to induce controlled precipitation of coherent L1₂ nano‐precipitates within the ductile fcc lamellae of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA will fortify phase boundaries, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance while preserving ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA exhibiting a dual‐phase lamellar microstructure composed of fcc and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Subject the as‐cast alloy to an aging heat treatment at approximately 650°C for 8–10 hours to trigger the formation of fine, coherent L1₂ intermetallic nano‐precipitates within the fcc lamellae.
generation.conditions: Intermediate aging temperatures (roughly 500–700°C) and durations that promote nanoscale precipitate formation without overaging, with subsequent service under cyclic thermal fluctuations and long‐term mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed, coherent L1₂ nano‐precipitates within the fcc matrix that act as strong dislocation barriers and help stabilize the lamellar architecture.
generation.mechanism: The nano‐precipitates impede dislocation motion and retard grain boundary sliding, which improves yield strength and delays creep deformation. They also distribute strain more evenly, reducing localized stress and crack initiation, while careful control of aging avoids overaging that could embrittle the alloy. Additional electrochemical testing ensures that the precipitation does not detrimentally affect corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Approximately a 10–15% increase in yield strength and a lower creep rate under constant load, with maintained ductility comparable to the as‐cast state.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA has excellent tensile performance but exhibits limitations under prolonged high-temperature creep conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects depend critically on maintaining the aging treatment parameters within the specified window; deviations leading to overaging may produce coarse precipitates and embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: Exactly how the quantitative enhancements in creep resistance and potential effects on corrosion behavior will manifest remains to be empirically determined; additional optimization of aging parameters may be required.

cited_evidence.text: The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. A commonly adopted strategy to overcome this strength-ductility tradeoff is to develop multi-phase microstructures, involving at least one ductile/soft and one hard/strong phase, mixed in the appropriate proportion. Common examples include duplex alloys, such as 2205 stainless steel, which have a hard bcc phase to increase the strength of the alloy and a soft fcc phase to maintain the tensile ductility while deformation. The goal has been on fine-tuning the alloy composition and/or processing conditions in order to obtain a material with a good balance between ductility and strength. Eutectic alloys, often exhibiting a two-phase lamellar microstructure, offer such a possibility, and have been investigated for many years in different classes of alloys. Eutectic morphologies are characterized by the simultaneous growth of two (or more) phases from the liquid. A recently developed new class of eutectic HEAs (EHEAs), have attracted a lot of attention due to their promising mechanical properties. candidates.hypothesis: A post-casting aging treatment designed to induce a controlled precipitation of coherent L1₂ nano-precipitates within the ductile fcc phase of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA will fortify phase boundaries, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance while preserving ductility.
candidates.intervention: Subject the cast alloy to an aging heat treatment at 650°C for 8–10 hours to trigger the formation of fine, coherent L1₂ intermetallic nano-precipitates within the fcc lamellae.
candidates.changes: Specified a temperature range and duration for the aging treatment, discussed potential overaging and provided a plan for a parametric study to optimize precipitate size; acknowledged the need to monitor corrosion behavior.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing a minor micro‐alloying addition of 1–2 at.% hafnium (Hf) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will modify phase boundary chemistry and promote the formation of stable, nanoscale Hf‐rich precipitates at these boundaries, thereby enhancing high‐temperature strength, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior without degrading the inherent strength–ductility balance.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% Hf during melting and casting with a controlled rapid solidification/homogenization process designed to promote Hf segregation to phase boundaries and form evenly distributed Hf‐rich nano‐precipitates.
candidates.changes: Clarified the specific role and processing details of 1–2 at.% Hf addition; incorporated more precise rationales for controlling Hf segregation, specifying cooling protocols to avoid coarse, brittle intermetallics; and refined the predicted quantitative outcomes and mechanism based on reviewer feedback.

candidates.hypothesis: A post‐casting aging treatment designed to induce controlled precipitation of coherent L1₂ nano‐precipitates within the ductile fcc lamellae of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA will fortify phase boundaries, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance while preserving ductility.
candidates.intervention: Subject the as‐cast alloy to an aging heat treatment at approximately 650°C for 8–10 hours to trigger the formation of fine, coherent L1₂ intermetallic nano‐precipitates within the fcc lamellae.
candidates.changes: Enhanced the definition of aging treatment parameters, clearly specifying the temperature and duration; discussed risks of overaging and added mention of complementary corrosion testing to meet reviewer concerns.

candidates.hypothesis: Depositing a thin, uniform HEA coating of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 via laser metal deposition (LMD) onto conventional fastener substrates will impart significant improvements in surface corrosion resistance and creep behavior under extreme thermal cycling, thereby enhancing the overall performance and longevity of fasteners.
candidates.intervention: Utilize LMD to deposit a ~100–200 µm thick, dense, well‐adherent HEA coating of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (or a slightly compositionally tailored variant) on fastener surfaces, followed by a post‐deposition heat treatment at ~900°C for 10 hours to optimize the coating microstructure and promote a graded interfacial layer.
candidates.changes: Expanded the description of interfacial quality including graded interlayers to address potential thermal expansion mismatches and adhesion issues; specified the coating thickness range and added details on post-deposition treatments to improve the coating’s integrity, as suggested by reviewers.

candidates.hypothesis: Cryogenic rolling followed by a controlled annealing treatment can refine the eutectic lamellar microstructure of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA, thereby enhancing its strength–ductility balance, reducing room-temperature creep rate, and improving surface corrosion resistance.
candidates.intervention: Subject the alloy to cryogenic rolling at −196°C with a total reduction of 20–25% at a strain rate of ~10^−2 s^−1, followed by a tailored annealing treatment at 700°C for 1 hour to enable controlled recovery and partial phase decomposition.
candidates.changes: Expanded the discussion of the trade-off between cryogenic rolling–induced damage and annealing recovery; detailed the specific processing parameters and the role of refined lamellar spacing in enhancing both mechanical and corrosion properties, as highlighted by reviewer suggestions.

major_issues: The mechanism for significantly improving creep performance via a thin (100–200 μm) coating remains uncertain because creep is largely a bulk property. Additional justification or data are needed to confirm the coating’s efficacy under prolonged high-temperature loading.
minor_issues: Further details on the chemical homogeneity and microstructural control of the deposited layer are not fully described.
The interplay between the coating’s thermal expansion and that of the substrate under extreme thermal cycles is acknowledged but merits deeper analysis.
fixes: Provide direct high-temperature creep data or references demonstrating substantial creep life improvements from similar thin HEA coatings.
Address potential mismatches in thermal expansion between the substrate and the coating, and demonstrate how the proposed graded interface resolves or mitigates these stresses.
evidence_needs: Experimental verification (e.g., creep testing with coated vs. uncoated fasteners at relevant service temperatures and stresses) to confirm the claimed 20–30% corrosion improvement and creep-life extension.
Residual stress measurements (e.g., XRD stress analysis) at the coating-substrate interface to ensure that thermal cycling does not induce early delamination.

minor_issues: Details on the cooling protocols to ensure controlled Hf segregation and avoid coarse intermetallic formation are not fully elaborated.
fixes: Include a more explicit process window (solidification rate, homogenization temperature/time) to ensure the stable formation of fine Hf-rich precipitates.
evidence_needs: Quantitative creep data at elevated temperatures to validate the predicted 10–15% reduction in creep rate.
Phase characterization via TEM or atom probe tomography to confirm uniform distribution of Hf-rich nano-precipitates.

fixes: Add electrochemical testing protocols (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to rule out potential corrosion trade-offs from the nano-precipitation.
evidence_needs: High-temperature creep data, along with microstructural examination (TEM) confirming fine L1₂ precipitates and their stability over time.
